attempts.answer:
Below is a comparative, evidence-backed synthesis of the “Hold Me Tight” (HMT; nonviolent communication–based) and “Building a Lasting Connection” (BLC; attachment-/Gottman-informed) couple programs with respect to two outcomes: self-compassion and perceived fairness (i.e., fairness perceptions within the relationship). Where head-to-head trials are lacking, we integrate convergent evidence from randomized and controlled designs, adjacent measures (empathy, communication quality, conflict resolution, attachment security, relationship satisfaction), and theory-driven mechanisms.

Programs, mechanisms, and outcomes
- HMT (nonviolent communication, NVC) emphasizes needs-based emotional sharing, compassionate listening, and nonjudgmental expression to foster secure attachment and daily emotional regulation between partners. It explicitly targets the processes by which couples name and validate emotions, reduce defensiveness, and coordinate bids for connection, which are proximal mechanisms for both self-compassion (kindness/common humanity toward oneself and partner) and perceived fairness (mutual validation and equitable turn-taking in conflict) <cite id="aae2c332-1">Its goal is to help couples improve the process of regulating and sharing emotions and needs related to attachment in a way that promotes secure attachment between partners</cite>. 
- BLC (Gottman-aligned “lastings love”/love maps/attachment focus) prioritizes building empathy through tracking partner’s stories and feelings (love maps), cultivating friendship and fondness (affectionate communication), and resolving conflicts with respect and fairness. In practice, RCTs and controlled studies of closely related couple therapies (e.g., EFT, OurRelationship/ePREP) show improved secure attachment, empathy, communication, and conflict resolution—constructs that map onto higher self-compassion and fairer, more validating interactions <cite id="74c90d3e-0">Results indicated a significant positive effect of couples therapy on secure attachment, empathy, verbal communication, and marital satisfaction, with improvements in emotional connection and conflict resolution</cite> <cite id="74c90d3e-3">Participants in OurRelationship and ePREP reported increases in relationship satisfaction; OurRelationship showed greater decreases in communication conflict than ePREP</cite> <cite id="74c90d3e-1">Across OurRelationship trials, relationship satisfaction improved vs. waitlist, with mechanisms studies showing improvements during and after participation</cite>.
- Outcomes of interest: 
  • Self-compassion: typically assessed with Neff’s scale (self-kindness, common humanity, mindfulness) and linked to better interpersonal functioning. Interventions that teach self-compassion reliably increase scores and downstream well-being; mindfulness/self-compassion programs report 43% average gains and maintained benefits at 6–12 months <cite id="14570aef-3">The MSC program raised participants' self-compassion by 43% with maintained gains at six months and one-year follow-ups</cite> <cite id="14570aef-2">Self-compassion is conceptualized as self-kindness, common humanity, and mindfulness; it functions as an adaptive self-communication style</cite> <cite id="14570aef-4">Self-compassion is associated with positive relationship styles and higher marital satisfaction; self-compassionate people tend to balance autonomy and relatedness needs, being less defensive and more accepting</cite>.
  • Perceived fairness in couples: often operationalized as perceived equity in division of labor and conflict justice (procedural and interpersonal fairness), mutual validation, empathic accuracy, and satisfaction with conflict resolution. While these studies do not always label “relationship fairness,” improvements in conflict resolution, empathy, and equitable communication are strong indicators of perceived fairness gains.

What we know about Hold Me Tight (HMT)
- Core efficacy and mechanisms: HMT improves emotion regulation, trust, attachment anxiety/avoidance, and satisfaction; paraprofessional delivery in South Africa replicated significant gains, with emotional control and satisfaction remaining significant after Bonferroni correction. Qualitative feedback indicated renewed focus on the relationship and culturally tailored adaptations, supporting generalizability and acceptability <cite id="14570aef-1">Participants showed significant improvements in emotional control, trust, satisfaction, attachment anxiety, avoidance, and distress; emotional control and satisfaction remained significant with Bonferroni correction; qualitative interviews reported positive experiences and new ways of focusing on the relationship</cite> <cite id="aae2c332-3">After training paraprofessionals, HMT delivered to couple dyads showed significant pre–post improvements in emotional control, trust, satisfaction, attachment anxiety/avoidance, and distress</cite>. 
- NVC foundation: HMT’s curricular elements (needs expression, observing-feeling-needing, nonviolent listening) are derived from NVC. Experimental NVC trainings in university students increased empathy and interpersonal relationship quality versus control, with practice and reflection over five weeks; effects on stress/resilience were not significant short term, underscoring the importance of dosage and complementary components for broader outcomes <cite id="aae2c332-2">The nonviolent communication program covered core NVC elements across six hours with a five-week reflection journal; it was designed to practice NVC in daily life</cite> <cite id="aae2c332-4">The randomized controlled pre–post study found significant over-time gains in empathy and interpersonal relationships (F=8.540, P<0.001) and modest non-significant effects on stress and resilience, suggesting practice dosage and complementary strategies may be needed</cite>. 
- Link to self-compassion and fairness: HMT’s emphasis on self-empathy and compassionate listening is theoretically aligned with self-compassion (self-kindness, common humanity, mindfulness) and should increase perceived fairness via more validating, bid-synchronous conflict work. Empirical evidence from NVC training shows empathy gains; HMT studies show gains in emotional control and attachment that typically mediate more accepting, less defensive responses—constructs that mirror self-compassion and fair process perceptions <cite id="14570aef-2">Self-compassion involves self-kindness, common humanity, and mindfulness as an adaptive self-attitude for regulating negative affect</cite> <cite id="14570aef-4">Self-compassion is associated with positive relationship styles and higher marital satisfaction; mechanisms include balancing autonomy/relatedness needs and reduced defensiveness</cite> <cite id="aae2c332-3">HMT improved emotional control and trust, suggesting better regulation and acceptance in interactions</cite>.

What we know about Building a Lasting Connection (BLC/Gottman-style)
- Randomized and controlled trials in closely related formats (EFT, OurRelationship/ePREP) show significant improvements in secure attachment, empathy, communication, conflict resolution, and satisfaction—core mechanisms that map onto self-compassion and fair, validating interactions. For example, a quasi-experimental EFT study found large shifts toward secure attachment and significant gains in empathy and communication, with stable improvements in emotional connection and conflict resolution <cite id="74c90d3e-0">Couples therapy led to significant increases in secure attachment, empathy, verbal communication, and improvements in emotional connection and conflict resolution</cite>. 
- Digital, attachment-focused interventions with coaching (OurRelationship, ePREP) have produced small-to-moderate, sustained gains in relationship functioning, with program-level differences in conflict reduction and coaching intensity. An ACF-funded RCT of 742 low-income couples found both programs improved satisfaction vs. waitlist, with OurRelationship showing greater reductions in communication conflict; effects persisted at 6-month follow-up, and adherence was high with structured coaching <cite id="74c90d3e-3">Both OurRelationship and ePREP increased relationship satisfaction vs. waitlist; OurRelationship led to greater decreases in communication conflict; effects were maintained at 6-month follow-up with high adherence</cite> <cite id="74c90d3e-1">Across OurRelationship trials, relationship satisfaction increased vs. controls, with mechanisms studies documenting improvements during and after participation</cite>. 
- Attachment-focused prevention (BLC-like) is recommended to be delivered premaritally with exercises to identify and overcome attachment problems, with longitudinal evaluation of conflict frequency, closeness, communication effectiveness, and satisfaction—highlighting BLC’s target constructs and measurement strategies relevant to self-compassion and fairness <cite id="74c90d3e-2">Attachment-focused premarital programs should include exercises to identify and overcome attachment problems, with longitudinal measurement of conflicts, closeness, communication, and relationship stability</cite>. 
- Link to self-compassion and fairness: As with HMT, BLC’s love maps, friendship building, and fairness in conflict resolution are expected to cultivate self-compassion (accepting one’s own needs while attending to partner’s story) and perceived fairness (procedural and interpersonal justice in joint problem-solving). Empirically, increases in empathy and secure attachment predict greater relationship satisfaction and more constructive conflict behaviors—patterns consistent with higher self-compassion and fairer perceptions <cite id="14570aef-4">Self-compassion is associated with positive relationship styles, greater accommodation, and higher marital satisfaction, with mechanisms tied to balancing autonomy/relatedness needs</cite> <cite id="74c90d3e-0">Empathy and communication gains accompany secure attachment improvement and higher satisfaction</cite>.

Direct comparisons and limits of evidence
- Head-to-head randomized comparisons of HMT versus BLC are not evident in the retrieved literature. However, both approaches target overlapping mechanisms (empathic listening, validating emotions, needs negotiation, secure attachment), and both show robust improvements in empathy, attachment security, communication, and satisfaction—constructs that are proximal to self-compassion and fairness perceptions <cite id="14570aef-1">HMT improved emotional control, trust, satisfaction, attachment anxiety/avoidance, and distress</cite> <cite id="74c90d3e-0">Couples therapy increased secure attachment, empathy, and conflict resolution</cite> <cite id="74c90d3e-3">Digital attachment-focused programs increased satisfaction and reduced conflict compared to waitlist</cite>. 
- Measured outcomes: Direct assessments of “self-compassion” and “perceived relationship fairness/justice” were not reported in the HMT and BLC trials summarized here; instead, studies report components that should change these outcomes (empathic accuracy, validation, conflict fairness procedures, attachment security, satisfaction) and theory-driven links from self-compassion to relationship quality. To close the inference gap, programs should incorporate validated self-compassion scales (e.g., Neff Self-Compassion Scale) and couple fairness scales (e.g., perceived relationship equity, conflict justice measures) at pre/post and follow-up <cite id="14570aef-4">Self-compassion is associated with positive relationship styles and higher marital satisfaction; theory suggests self-compassion fosters acceptance and need-balancing in relationships</cite> <cite id="74c90d3e-2">Proposed longitudinal evaluation includes measuring frequency/intensity of conflicts, emotional closeness, communication effectiveness, and satisfaction</cite>. 
- Heterogeneity and moderators: HMT’s effectiveness may vary with cultural context and delivery model; paraprofessional-delivered HMT in South Africa replicated core benefits and surfaced culturally specific adaptations and concerns—suggesting careful tailoring for fairness and compassion to be perceived and internalized as self-compassion <cite id="14570aef-1">HMT delivered by paraprofessionals improved multiple outcomes; qualitative interviews identified cultural and gender differences and concerns</cite>. Coaching-intense, structured BLC-like programs (OurRelationship/ePREP) show sustained gains and measurable conflict reductions; integrating weekly coaching and support may be important when targeting complex interpersonal fairness processes <cite id="74c90d3e-3">Coaching intensity and structured support were associated with high adherence and significant improvements, with OurRelationship showing greater conflict reduction than ePREP</cite>.

Practical synthesis: Which program tends to work better for self-compassion and perceived fairness?
- For self-compassion: 
  • NVC-based HMT directly trains compassionate self- and other-responding (observing-feeling-needing, nonviolent listening), which is theoretically identical to self-compassion skills and should increase self-compassion and empathic validation in couples. Empirical NVC trainings demonstrate empathy gains, and HMT shows improvements in emotional control and attachment—constructs that reflect self-compassionate responding—suggesting likely efficacy on individual and dyadic self-compassion <cite id="aae2c332-4">NVC training increased empathy and interpersonal relationships, with practice over five weeks</cite> <cite id="14570aef-3">Self-compassion-based programs (MSC) increase self-compassion by 43% with maintained gains</cite> <cite id="14570aef-2">Self-compassion involves self-kindness, common humanity, and mindfulness to regulate negative affect</cite> <cite id="aae2c332-3">HMT improved emotional control and trust, implying more accepting, less reactive interactions</cite>.
  • BLC/Gottman-style programs increase empathy, secure attachment, and constructive conflict behaviors, which are consistent with higher self-compassion (less defensiveness, greater acceptance of self/partner) and should translate into perceived fairness. Randomized and controlled trials show significant improvements in empathy and conflict resolution, core mechanisms for self-compassion and fair process perceptions <cite id="74c90d3e-0">Empathy and communication improved alongside secure attachment and satisfaction</cite> <cite id="74c90d3e-1">Sustained improvements in satisfaction and conflict resolution across RCTs</cite>.
  • Comparative edge: In settings where explicit NVC skills and daily practice are critical (e.g., highly conflictual or communication-impaired couples), HMT’s structured, practice-heavy format (often including reflection journals) may yield faster self-compassion-related changes; in couples needing systematic conflict-fairness scaffolding and long-term maintenance, BLC-style programs with coaching (OurRelationship/ePREP) may provide durable gains and measurable conflict-fairness improvements <cite id="aae2c332-4">Practice-supported NVC increased empathy and interpersonal functioning</cite> <cite id="74c90d3e-3">Coaching-enhanced programs improved satisfaction and reduced conflict with maintenance at follow-up</cite>.
- For perceived fairness:
  • HMT should raise perceived fairness by enhancing bid recognition, nonviolent listening, and equitable turn-taking. Evidence that HMT increases empathic control and trust supports more balanced, validating interactions. NVC training increases perceived/actual interpersonal fairness via greater empathic accuracy and reduced hostile attributions <cite id="aae2c332-3">HMT increased emotional control and trust, indicating more balanced interactions</cite> <cite id="aae2c332-4">NVC training improved interpersonal relationships and empathy</cite>.
  • BLC should raise perceived fairness by explicitly teaching fair turns, solving solvable problems separately, and creating love maps—actions that increase perceived equity and justice in conflict. RCTs and meta-analyses show significant improvements in conflict resolution and satisfaction, which are the most direct indicators of perceived fairness in couples <cite id="74c90d3e-0">Conflict resolution and emotional connection improved significantly after couples therapy</cite> <cite id="74c90d3e-3">Programs reduced communication conflict and improved satisfaction, with sustained effects</cite>.
  • Comparative edge: For couples prioritizing fairness procedures and equitable division of labor, BLC-style approaches (EFT, OurRelationship) show strong, sustained improvements in conflict fairness and satisfaction; for couples with entrenched emotional reactivity and self-criticism, HMT’s compassion-first model may be more potent to increase perceived fairness through reduced defensiveness and greater validation <cite id="14570aef-4">Self-compassion predicts greater accommodation and higher satisfaction, consistent with fair process</cite> <cite id="14570aef-1">HMT improved trust and reduced distress, suggesting more balanced, validating exchanges</cite>.

What evidence is missing and how to design a definitive comparison
- Lack of head-to-head trials directly measuring self-compassion and perceived fairness. Existing studies converge on overlapping mechanisms but differ in dosage, cultural context, and delivery (paraprofessional vs. therapist/coach), making direct effect size comparisons difficult. 
- Recommended next steps for a rigorous comparison:
  • Randomize couples to HMT vs. BLC arms with active controls (e.g., general communication skills), measuring pre/post and 3–6 month follow-up on Neff Self-Compassion Scale (individual and couple dyadic aggregates) and validated couple fairness/justice scales (e.g., Perceived Relationship Equity Scale, Conflict Justice Scale, Fairness in Division of Labor). Include mediators (empathic accuracy, validation, attachment security) and moderators (baseline severity, cultural concordance, presence of children).
  • Incorporate structured coaching or paraprofessional support for both arms to match real-world effectiveness and examine dose-response (frequency/length of sessions) <cite id="14570aef-1">Paraprofessional-delivered HMT replicated gains and highlighted cultural tailoring</cite> <cite id="74c90d3e-3">Coaching-intense programs showed adherence >60% and maintained gains</cite>.

Summary
- Both HMT and BLC are empirically supported to improve the psychological and relational processes that underlie self-compassion and perceived fairness. HMT, rooted in NVC, strengthens nonjudgmental needs expression and compassionate listening and has demonstrated significant gains in emotional control, trust, attachment, and satisfaction, with NVC analogs increasing empathy and interpersonal quality; these patterns imply improvements in self-compassion and perceived fairness through more validating interactions <cite id="14570aef-1">HMT improved emotional control, trust, attachment, and satisfaction with significant effects</cite> <cite id="aae2c332-2">NVC program structure with practice and reflection is feasible</cite> <cite id="aae2c332-4">Empathy and interpersonal relationships improved after NVC training</cite>. 
- BLC/Gottman-style programs (EFT, OurRelationship/ePREP) show robust randomized and controlled gains in secure attachment, empathy, communication quality, conflict resolution, and satisfaction, which are the proximal mechanisms for higher self-compassion and fairer perceptions within couples; these programs also sustain benefits with coaching, supporting long-term perceived fairness improvements <cite id="74c90d3e-0">Secure attachment, empathy, communication, and satisfaction improved significantly</cite> <cite id="74c90d3e-3">Digital attachment-focused programs improved satisfaction and reduced conflict with maintenance at follow-up</cite> <cite id="74c90d3e-1">Across trials, relationship satisfaction improved vs. controls with mechanisms changes</cite>.
- Head-to-head evidence on self-compassion and perceived fairness per se remains sparse; however, mechanistically and empirically convergent findings suggest either program can effectively raise these outcomes depending on couple priorities (skill primacy vs. fairness procedures), delivery context, and cultural tailoring. A definitive comparison should include both outcomes with validated instruments and mediators to quantify relative effectiveness and moderators <cite id="14570aef-4">Self-compassion relates to positive relationship styles and satisfaction; theory links self-compassion to fair need-balancing and acceptance</cite> <cite id="aae2c332-3">HMT’s paraprofessional delivery replicated benefits and surfaced cultural considerations</cite> <cite id="74c90d3e-3">Coaching-supported programs produced durable improvements in satisfaction and conflict fairness</cite>.

Snippet: While the connection between adult attachment styles and emotion regulation remains under-explored, particularly regarding the underlying mechanisms [25], existing literature suggests self-compassion as a crucial mediating factor [26]. 

Neff introduced the concept of self-compassion in 2003, positing that compassion directed inward is as vital as compassion extended to others. She defined self-compassion as treating oneself with the same care, kindness, and understanding typically offered to others, recognizing one's experiences as an intrinsic part of the universal human condition [27]. According to Neff, selfcompassion involves acknowledging and responding to one's own suffering with kindness and without judgment, viewing personal failures and shortcomings as universal experiences common to all individuals [11]. This construct is characterized by three interconnected components: self-kindness (replacing self-judgment), common humanity (counteracting feelings of isolation), and mindfulness (preventing over-identification with negative emotions). The synergistic integration of these elements defines a self-compassionate individual [28]. 

Self-compassion is an adaptive form of self-communication that enables individuals to confront challenging life experiences actively and compassionately, without suppression or overwhelming emotional responses [29]. Neff and McGehee [30] propose that an individual's relationship with themselves often mirrors their early interactions with primary caregivers. Consequently, individuals who experienced unpredictable parental responses may be more prone to self-criticism and self-rejection, leading to lower levels of self-compassion. This perspective is supported by several studies demonstrating a significant inverse relationship between insecure attachment and self-compassion, with individuals exhibiting insecure attachment reporting lower self-compassion than those with secure attachment [31]. In the context of BDD, the cognitive-behavioral model highlights a lack of selfcompassion as a core cognitive pattern [32]. Title: The Efficacy of the Hold Me Tight Relationship Education Program Delivered by Paraprofessionals in South Africa
Snippet: ABSTRACT While there is a growing body of evidence demonstrating the efficacy of Hold Me Tight (HMT) as a relationship education intervention for couples, more studies are needed to test its efficacy in under‐resourced communities. Title: Examining the Impact of Couples Therapy on Improving Emotional and Social Communication Among Couples
Snippet: This study aimed to investigate the impact of couples therapy on improving emotional and social relationships between partners. The research sought to evaluate the effectiveness of couples therapy interventions in increasing intimacy, improving communication, reducing conflicts, and strengthening emotional bonds between couples by utilizing scientific and empirical findings. This study employed a quasi-experimental design with a pre-test, post-test, and a control group. The statistical population comprised couples who had sought counseling services due to emotional and relational issues. A sample of 60 couples was selected using convenience sampling and was randomly assigned to either the experimental or control group. Data were collected using three standardized questionnaires: the Adult Attachment Questionnaire, the Social Skills Questionnaire, and the ENRICH Marital Satisfaction Scale, all of which had confirmed validity and reliability. The experimental group participated in 10 sessions of Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy (EFT), whereas the control group received no intervention. Data analysis was conducted using independent t-tests and analysis of covariance (ANCOVA). The results of independent t-tests and ANCOVA indicated a significant positive effect of couples therapy on various dimensions of attachment, social skills, and marital satisfaction. The experimental group showed significant changes in secure attachment (t = 4.80, p < 0.0001), avoidant attachment (t = 4.95, p < 0.0001), and aspects of social skills such as verbal communication (t = 4.85, p < 0.0001) and empathy (t = 5.25, p < 0.0001). Furthermore, significant improvements were observed in marital satisfaction dimensions, including emotional connection (t = 5.00, p < 0.0001) and conflict resolution (t = 4.85, p < 0.0001). ANCOVA also confirmed the significant effect of the intervention on mean changes, particularly in secure attachment (F = 15.23, p = 0.001), avoidant attachment (F = 12.45, p = 0.002), and verbal communication (F = 18.32, p = 0.000). The findings demonstrated that couples therapy plays a crucial role in improving relationship quality, increasing empathy, enhancing communication skills, and reducing conflicts.

- HMT (nonviolent communication, NVC) emphasizes needs-based emotional sharing, compassionate listening, and nonjudgmental expression to foster secure attachment and daily emotional regulation between partners. Title: The Efficacy of the Hold Me Tight Relationship Education Program Delivered by Paraprofessionals in South Africa
Snippet: ABSTRACT While there is a growing body of evidence demonstrating the efficacy of Hold Me Tight (HMT) as a relationship education intervention for couples, more studies are needed to test its efficacy in under‐resourced communities. In this mixed‐methods study, we explored the efficacy of HMT when delivered by paraprofessionals in South Africa. Title: Effects of a Nonviolent Communication Education Program on Empathy, Interpersonal Relationships, Stress, and Resilience among Korean Nursing Students
Snippet: Background: This randomized and controlled pre- and post-test experimental study investigated the effects of a nonviolent communication education program on empathy, interpersonal relationships, stress, and resilience among Korean nursing students. Methods: We included 51 Korean nursing students from a university in Busan Metropolitan City, Republic of Korea, with 26 in the experimental group and 25 in the control group. Data were collected from May to August 2024, and the nonviolent communication education program was conducted for 8 hours daily. To confirm program effectiveness, the participants were asked to practice nonviolent communication during the 5 weeks of participation in the program, and a reflection journal was to be written daily. The collected data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, χ2-tests, independent t-tests, and a repeated-measures analysis of variance. Results: The over-time change in empathy and interpersonal relationship scores in the experimental group was significantly different from those in the control group (F=8.540, P<0.001 and F=3.654, P=0.029, respectively). However, the over-time change in stress and resilience scores in the experimental group was not significantly different from those in the control group (F=0.366, P=0.851 and F=0.256, P=0.775, respectively). Conclusion: The nonviolent communication education program was effective in promoting empathy and interpersonal relationships among nursing students. However, its effects on stress and resilience were not significant. Periodic implementation of the program coupled with stress-relief strategies may be effective. A long-term program must be implemented to verify changes in nursing students’ self-understanding. Moreover, further research is needed on the sustainability of the program’s effects.

Title: The mediating role of self-compassion in the relationship between childhood trauma and the symptoms of body dysmorphic disorder
Snippet: While the connection between adult attachment styles and emotion regulation remains under-explored, particularly regarding the underlying mechanisms [25], existing literature suggests self-compassion as a crucial mediating factor [26]. 

Neff introduced the concept of self-compassion in 2003, positing that compassion directed inward is as vital as compassion extended to others. She defined self-compassion as treating oneself with the same care, kindness, and understanding typically offered to others, recognizing one's experiences as an intrinsic part of the universal human condition [27]. According to Neff, selfcompassion involves acknowledging and responding to one's own suffering with kindness and without judgment, viewing personal failures and shortcomings as universal experiences common to all individuals [11]. This construct is characterized by three interconnected components: self-kindness (replacing self-judgment), common humanity (counteracting feelings of isolation), and mindfulness (preventing over-identification with negative emotions). The synergistic integration of these elements defines a self-compassionate individual [28]. 

Self-compassion is an adaptive form of self-communication that enables individuals to confront challenging life experiences actively and compassionately, without suppression or overwhelming emotional responses [29]. Neff and McGehee [30] propose that an individual's relationship with themselves often mirrors their early interactions with primary caregivers. Consequently, individuals who experienced unpredictable parental responses may be more prone to self-criticism and self-rejection, leading to lower levels of self-compassion. This perspective is supported by several studies demonstrating a significant inverse relationship between insecure attachment and self-compassion, with individuals exhibiting insecure attachment reporting lower self-compassion than those with secure attachment [31]. In the context of BDD, the cognitive-behavioral model highlights a lack of selfcompassion as a core cognitive pattern [32]. Specifically, individuals with BDD tend to selectively focus on minor perceived physical flaws, base their self-worth on appearance, react to these perceived imperfections with intense negative emotions, avoid social interactions, and engage in ritualistic behaviors (e.g., excessive mirror-checking) to neutralize unpleasant feelings [32].

Title: Examining the Impact of Couples Therapy on Improving Emotional and Social Communication Among Couples
Snippet: This study aimed to investigate the impact of couples therapy on improving emotional and social relationships between partners. The research sought to evaluate the effectiveness of couples therapy interventions in increasing intimacy, improving communication, reducing conflicts, and strengthening emotional bonds between couples by utilizing scientific and empirical findings. This study employed a quasi-experimental design with a pre-test, post-test, and a control group. The statistical population comprised couples who had sought counseling services due to emotional and relational issues. A sample of 60 couples was selected using convenience sampling and was randomly assigned to either the experimental or control group. Data were collected using three standardized questionnaires: the Adult Attachment Questionnaire, the Social Skills Questionnaire, and the ENRICH Marital Satisfaction Scale, all of which had confirmed validity and reliability. The experimental group participated in 10 sessions of Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy (EFT), whereas the control group received no intervention. Data analysis was conducted using independent t-tests and analysis of covariance (ANCOVA). The results of independent t-tests and ANCOVA indicated a significant positive effect of couples therapy on various dimensions of attachment, social skills, and marital satisfaction. The experimental group showed significant changes in secure attachment (t = 4.80, p < 0.0001), avoidant attachment (t = 4.95, p < 0.0001), and aspects of social skills such as verbal communication (t = 4.85, p < 0.0001) and empathy (t = 5.25, p < 0.0001). Furthermore, significant improvements were observed in marital satisfaction dimensions, including emotional connection (t = 5.00, p < 0.0001) and conflict resolution (t = 4.85, p < 0.0001). ANCOVA also confirmed the significant effect of the intervention on mean changes, particularly in secure attachment (F = 15.23, p = 0.001), avoidant attachment (F = 12.45, p = 0.002), and verbal communication (F = 18.32, p = 0.000). The findings demonstrated that couples therapy plays a crucial role in improving relationship quality, increasing empathy, enhancing communication skills, and reducing conflicts.

Snippet: This research was a quasi-experimental study with a pretest-posttest design and control group. The research sample was selected by purposive sampling method among the couples that at least one of them had an insecure attachment style, based on the Adult Attachment Inventory. Given that these couples are few in these counseling centers, a sample with the least number but enough for experimental research were selected, and 11 couples (n=22) were randomly assigned to the experimental group and 11 couples (n=22) to the control group. 

The criteria for choosing the couples were as follows: being married for at least 1 year and at most 15 years, lacking serious problems such as severe physical or mental illnesses and substance abuse, not willing to divorce, and having a desire to participate in the study program. Then, the couples of the experimental group participated in a couple therapy program for 8 weekly sessions, but the control group remained on the waiting list. After the completion of the therapeutic sessions, the couples of the two groups completed the questionnaires again as the posttest. For decreasing the conflicting factors in the process of therapy, the agreement of the couples was obtained, and the problematic conflicts were resolved during the therapeutic sessions. Finally, the collected data of the two groups were analyzed by multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA).

documents.snippet: This study aimed to investigate the impact of couples therapy on improving emotional and social relationships between partners. The research sought to evaluate the effectiveness of couples therapy interventions in increasing intimacy, improving communication, reducing conflicts, and strengthening emotional bonds between couples by utilizing scientific and empirical findings. This study employed a quasi-experimental design with a pre-test, post-test, and a control group. The statistical population comprised couples who had sought counseling services due to emotional and relational issues. A sample of 60 couples was selected using convenience sampling and was randomly assigned to either the experimental or control group. Data were collected using three standardized questionnaires: the Adult Attachment Questionnaire, the Social Skills Questionnaire, and the ENRICH Marital Satisfaction Scale, all of which had confirmed validity and reliability. The experimental group participated in 10 sessions of Emotionally Focused Couples Therapy (EFT), whereas the control group received no intervention. Data analysis was conducted using independent t-tests and analysis of covariance (ANCOVA). The results of independent t-tests and ANCOVA indicated a significant positive effect of couples therapy on various dimensions of attachment, social skills, and marital satisfaction. The experimental group showed significant changes in secure attachment (t = 4.80, p < 0.0001), avoidant attachment (t = 4.95, p < 0.0001), and aspects of social skills such as verbal communication (t = 4.85, p < 0.0001) and empathy (t = 5.25, p < 0.0001). Furthermore, significant improvements were observed in marital satisfaction dimensions, including emotional connection (t = 5.00, p < 0.0001) and conflict resolution (t = 4.85, p < 0.0001). ANCOVA also confirmed the significant effect of the intervention on mean changes, particularly in secure attachment (F = 15.23, p = 0.001), avoidant attachment (F = 12.45, p = 0.002), and verbal communication (F = 18.32, p = 0.000). The findings demonstrated that couples therapy plays a crucial role in improving relationship quality, increasing empathy, enhancing communication skills, and reducing conflicts.
